title: Patience in the Quran
hookLine: the Quran praises patient endurance and prayer
carry: patience is at the first stroke

lines: A WOMAN WEEPING AT A GRAVE.
cards: A woman is weeping at a grave. A man passing by stops and tells her to fear God and be patient. She snaps at him: leave me alone, you haven't been hit by what hit me.
She doesn't know who he is. Later someone tells her: that was the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. She hurries to his door to apologize, and finds no guards there, just the man.
And what he says to her, in the hadith collection of al-Bukhari, is one short sentence about when patience counts.

teach.b: First, the word. In Arabic it's sabr.
English often says patience, but in one verse of the second chapter, Pickthall reaches for a sturdier word: "O ye who believe! Seek help in steadfastness and prayer. Lo! Allah is with the steadfast."
Not waiting quietly in a line. Standing your ground while something hard goes on. Second, the pairing.

In that verse, sabr comes with prayer. Endurance and turning to God are offered together, as help, not as a test passed on your own strength. And the verse ends with a place to stand: God is with the steadfast.
Third, the honesty. Two verses later, the Quran doesn't promise an easy life.
People will be tried, it says, with some fear and hunger, with loss of wealth and lives and crops. Then: give good news to the steadfast. Sabr isn't the absence of hardship.
It's what someone does in the middle of one. Fourth, back to the grave.
The Prophet's answer to the woman, as al-Bukhari records it, is that patience is at the first stroke. Not weeks later, once the worst has passed. At the first blow.
It isn't a ban on tears; in another hadith, the Prophet weeps at a death himself.
Sabr, in this reading, is the first moment's choice of how to meet what hit you: with tears if they come, but without turning on the person beside you, or on God.

how: Muslims speak of sabr as a virtue to practice in hardship, in daily duties and in restraint, and pair it with prayer, as the Quran does.

o: never letting yourself cry over a loss
patience that holds steady at the first blow
quiet waiting until hard times pass by

games.q: what's inside sabr — tap the pairs.

s: the Quran promises the steadfast a life free of loss
it says people will be tried with fear, hunger and loss, then gives good news to the steadfast.
in this verse, sabr is paired with prayer
in the hadith, patience means never weeping
the Prophet weeps at a death himself; patience is how the first blow is met.

games.q: you're the woman at the grave. you snapped at a stranger, and now you learn he was the Prophet. what do you do?
o: go to his door and explain you didn't recognize him.
games.why: she goes to his door, finds no guards, and he tells her that patience is at the first stroke.

practice: Think back to the last small blow you took, a sharp word, bad news, a plan that fell through, and remember its first second: the jolt, the heat, what you said or nearly said.
Replay that second slowly and let the feeling be there, and this time take one breath before anything else happens. That breath is a patient moment; rest in it.

wordCard.voice: Sabr: Arabic, patience, steadfastness. In the Quran it comes with prayer, and God is with the steadfast. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: patience, steadfastness; Pickthall renders it 'steadfastness' in Quran 2:153.

carryVoice: Your line: patience is at the first stroke. Tears can come, and the steadfast still stand. Day seven hundred twenty.
